Quetiapine 25-50mg (max 750mg/24hrs) or 
Risperidone 0.5-2mg (max 16mg/24hrs) 
 
Consider combination of lorazepam and promethazine OR 
olanzapine OR Quetiapine OR Risperidone if single agent 
ineffective 
Consider Injection 
 
*Lorazepam 0.5-2mg IM 
(max 4mg by oral or IM/24hrs) 
 
Give over 2-3 minutes 
Dilute 1:1 with water for injection or 0.9%NaCl before use 
*NB When administering IM Lorazepam, equipment necessary to maintain 
a patient airway and to support respiration should be available and used 
when necessary. 
 
Following injection, reconsider feasibility of 
administration of oral atypical antipsychotic 
as detailed above 
 
 
 
Repeat Lorazepam injection if necessary 
(Max 4mg by oral or IM/24hrs) 
 
Revert to vital sign monitoring 
Consider Injection 
 
*Lorazepam 0.5-2mg IM 
(max 4mg by oral or IM/24hrs) 
 
Give over 2-3 minutes 
Dilute 1:1 with water for injection or 0.9%NaCl before use 
*NB When administering IM Lorazepam, equipment necessary to maintain a 
patient airway and to support respiration should be available and used when 
necessary. 
 
Following injection, reconsider feasibility of 
administration of oral atypical antipsychotic as 
detailed above 
 
Occasionally: 
 IM Olanzapine 2 5-10mg as a single agent.  Reconstitute only 
with water for injection as per the NHSGGC Mental Health 
Partnerships Use of Olanzapine IM advice. 
Repeat injection(s) if necessary. 
Lorazepam: max 4mg by oral or IM/24hrs 
NB: If IM Olanzapine to be repeated- wait 2 hours 
 2.5-10mg, may be administered 2 hours after the first injection.  
The maximum daily dose of olanzapine (including oral olanzapine) 
is 20mg, with  not more than 3 injections in any 24-hour period) 
If olanzapine IM administered, wait 1 hour before administering 
an IM benzodiazepine 
If an IM benzodiazepine administered, the clinical status of the 
patient should be assessed and consultant advice obtained prior to 
IM Olanzapine being administered. 
Revert to vital sign monitoring 
 
Adolescents have developing brains and are vulnerable to side effects 
e.g. disinhibition due to the use of benzodiazepine medication.  
It is NEVER appropriate to use haloperidol in adolescents.

documents.title: Adrenal insufficiency in children, emergency and acute management guidance, paediatrics (239)
documents.content: Adrenal insufficiency in children, emergency and acute management guidance, paediatrics (239) ! Warning Objectives Standardisation of the emergency management of acutely unwell children with known or suspected adrenal insufficiency. Scope This clinical guidance should be used in children with known or suspected adrenal insufficiency who present acutely unwell. Conditions: Children on daily replacement hydrocortisone treatment, eg. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Congenital Adrenal Hypoplasia Addison’s disease Hypopituitarism eg congenital, brain tumour and post-radiotherapy Children on high dose glucocorticoid treatment (Prednisolone, Deflazacort, Dexamethasone, Vamorolone) eg Inflammatory conditions like inflammatory arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Source for guidance This clinical guidance adopts recommendations from the UK National Paediatric Adrenal Insufficiency Emergency Management Guidance developed by the British Society for Paediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes (2022). The British Society for Paediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes guidance has also been incorporated into the NICE guideline [NG243] Adrenal insufficiency: Identification and management (Published 28 th August 2024). EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT OF SUSPECTED ADRENAL CRISIS (SEVERE ILLNESS OR STRESS): REQUIRE IM OR IV HYDROCORTISONE Need for IM or IV hydrocortisone. DO NOT DELAY ADMINISTRATION OF IM or IV HYDROCORTISONE WITH SUSPECTED ADRENAL CRISIS.  PATIENTS WITH SUSPECTED ADRENAL CRISIS COULD DETERIORATE RAPIDLY EVEN IF APPEAR WELL. INITIAL MANAGEMENT OF SUSPECTED ADRENAL CRISIS Administer IV bolus or IM hydrocortisone Manage acute presentation as appropriate (treat the underlying cause) IM or initial IV bolus hydrocortisone doses for suspected adrenal crisis Age Dose of hydrocortisone (IM or initial IV bolus) Less than 1 year 25 mg 1 to 5 years 50 mg 6 years and over 100 mg Indications: Acutely unwell with diarrhoea and vomiting Reduced responsiveness or loss of consciousness Hypoglycaemia or new onset seizure in known or suspected adrenal insufficiency Painful fracture or fractures with significant deformity Significant burn Major trauma or severe shock (eg road traffic accident, head injury with loss of consciousness On arrival to hospital, check blood glucose as soon as possible. If blood glucose < 3 mmol/L, give 3 ml/kg of 10% dextrose as bolus. Recheck blood glucose in 15 min and repeat bolus if necessary. If shock or moderate to severe dehydration, give 10 ml/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride and repeat if necessary. Check electrolytes at presentation to inform fluid usage. SUBSEQUENT MANAGEMENT OF SUSPECTED ADRENAL CRISIS Following bolus of IV/IM hydrocortisone the child should be started on a hydrocortisone infusion Hydrocortisone infusion for acute illness Weight Total dose in 24 hours Infusion rate (50mg hydrocortisone in 50ml 0.9% sodium chloride) ≤10kg 25 mg 1 ml/hr 10.1 to 20kg 50 mg 2 ml/hr 20.1 to 40kg 100 mg 4 ml/hr 40.1 to 70kg 150 mg 6 ml/hr Over 70kg 200 mg 8 ml/hr To make up hydrocortisone infusion Add 50 mg hydrocortisone in 50 ml 0.9% sodium chloride Hydrocortisone infusion can run alongside 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% glucose or PlasmaLyte solutions Consider more concentrated infusions in those needing fluid restriction (eg 100 mg hydrocortisone in 50 ml 0.9% sodium chloride) Maintenance fluid type 0.9% sodium chloride / 5 % glucose is usually an appropriate starting point. Hyperkalaemia : Children with primary adrenal insufficiency can be hyperkalaemic at presentation or in an adrenal crisis because of mineralocorticoid deficiency. Emergency management of adrenal crisis with IV glucocorticoids and IV fluids (0.9% sodium chloride) will reduce potassium levels. Hyperkalaemia is potentially life-threatening and can lead to cardiac arrhythmias. Additional measures such as the use of IV calcium gluconate, nebulised salbutamol, IV insulin and glucose or IV bicarbonate and cation exchange resins should also be considered. 23 Hyponatraemia and fluids : Sodium chloride 0.9%/5% glucose is usually a good starting point for initial fluid management if the clinical and biochemical picture suggest that the low sodium has arisen primarily because of salt wasting. In primary adrenal insufficiency (eg Addison’s disease, Congenital adrenal hyperplasia), mineralocorticoid deficiency will cause hyponatraemia due to renal losses. In secondary adrenal insufficiency (eg hypopituitarism, patients with brain tumours or post-radiotherapy, patients on long term treatment dose of glucocorticoid eg Prednisolone, Deflazacort, Dexamethasone), cortisol deficiency can lead to a lack of free water clearance which can contribute to hyponatraemia. In this latter scenario (those with secondary adrenal insufficiency), a degree of fluid restriction may be more appropriate. Fludrocortisone is an oral mineralocorticoid used in primary adrenal insufficiency. The dose does not need adjustment in the event of a sick day episode or an adrenal crisis. If the child is unable to take oral medication then IV fluids may be required to maintain the salt and water balance depending on the clinical situation. However, the mineralocorticoid effect of hydrocortisone at stress doses is often sufficient to cover the mineralocorticoid requirement. Oral fludrocortisone should be re-commenced when able to tolerate oral medication. EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT OF SICK DAY EPISODE (MODERATE ILLNESS OR STRESS): REQUIRE ORAL SICK DAY DOSING Need for oral sick day dosing Indications: Acute infections/childhood illnesses with fever (usually not well enough to go to school) Vomiting or diarrhoea (only if tolerating oral medication and fluid but low threshold for consideration for IM or IV therapy) Oral sick day dosing based on weight. A guide to sick day dosing that can safely be used in the emergency setting is provided below. However, the actual dose may vary depending on the strength and preparation of the available hydrocortisone medication. Rounding up to the next 0.5 mg dosing is appropriate. Sick day dosing should be given for the duration of the illness. Patients own personalized sick day dosing plans from clinical review within the last 6 months (if available) can also be used. Patients should should be advised to ring primary medical team if no improvement after 48 hours or if further deterioration on oral sick day dosing following discharge from the hospital/A&E. For patients on treatment dose of glucocorticoid (eg Prednisolone, Deflazacort), a simple and safe approach is for additional sick day hydrocortisone to ensure adequate plasma cortisol levels throughout the day and night, on top of usual treatment dose of glucocorticoid (eg Prednisolone, Deflazacort). This is relevant as the half-life of Deflazacort is 1.5 to 1.9 hours; and the half-life of Prednisolone is 2.0 to 4.0 hours. The treatment dose of glucocorticoid (eg Prednisolone, Deflazacort) does not need to be altered during sick day episodes. Weight(kg) Sick day hydrocortisone: Dose Frequency 1 0.8 mg 4 x a day 2 1.2 mg 4 x a day 3 1.5 mg 4 x a day 4 2.0 mg 4 x a day 5 2.5 mg 4 x a day 6 2.5 mg 4 x a day 7 3.0 mg 4 x a day 8 3.0 mg 4 x a day 9 3.5 mg 4 x a day 10 4.0 mg 4 x a day 15 5.0 mg 4 x a day 20 6.0 mg 4 x a day 25 7.5 mg 4 x a day 30 7.5 mg 4 x a day 35 10.0 mg 4 x a day 40 10.0 mg 4 x a day 45 10.0 mg 4 x a day 50 10.0 mg 4 x a day 55 12.5 mg 4 x a day 60 12.5 mg 4 x a day 65 12.5 mg 4 x a day 70 15.0 mg 4 x a day 75 15.0 mg 4 x a day 80 15.0 mg 4 x a day 90 15.0 mg 4 x a day EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT OF SICK DAY EPISODE (MILD ILLNESS OR STRESS): NO NEED FOR SICK DAY DOSING No need for sick day dosing (ie no change to usual treatment) Indications: Mild cold or runny nose with no fever. Minor playground bumps and bruises Editorial Information Last reviewed: 10/01/2025 Next review date: 31/01/2029 Author(s): Jarod Wong, Avril Mason, Roisin Boyle. documents.title: Adrenal suppression secondary to exogenous glucocorticoid - guidance for children on long term steroid therapy (511)
documents.content: Adrenal suppression secondary to exogenous glucocorticoid - guidance for children on long term steroid therapy (511) ! Warning Objectives This document provides guidance on management and monitoring of children on long term steroids who at risk of secondary adrenal suppression. There is limited evidence in the area of monitoring/management during the discontinuation of long term steroid therapy. This guidance is developed to ensure safe practice, as there have been reported fatalities secondary to adrenal suppression. Background to condition Oral glucocorticoids (steroids) are widely used for their anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive properties in many conditions eg duchenne muscular dystrophy, juvenile idiopathic arthritis/chronic childhood rheumatic conditions, inflammatory bowel disease, atopic conditions, nephrotic syndrome, childhood cancers, solid organ transplant etc Physiological cortisol production is equivalent to approximately 10 mg/m 2 /day Hydrocortisone. Steroid equivalence for glucocorticoid activity 1 mg Prednisolone= 4 mg hydrocortisone 1 mg Triamcinolone= 4mg hydrocortisone 1 mg Methylprednisolone = 5mg hydrocortisone 1 mg Deflazacort= 6 mg hydrocortisone 1 mg Dexamethasone= 25 mg hydrocortisone Who is at risk? All pharmacological doses of oral steroid used clinically for treatment in current paediatric clinical practice are greater than physiological dose. Therefore, children treated with higher than physiological dose of steroid (> 2.5 mg/m 2 /day Prednisolone or > 10 mg/ m 2 /day hydrocortisone or equivalent) for greater than 4 weeks maybe at risk of secondary adrenal suppression. Continuous treatment for > 6 months will increase the risk. Children treated for > 12 months are at very high risk. Concurrent treatment with other forms of steroid eg intra-articular, inhaled, topical, nasal, eye drops will increase the risk. (Refer to separate guidance for monitoring of children on inhaled steroid) Repeated use of intra-articular, inhaled, topical, nasal, eye drop steroids may also lead to adrenal insufficiency. The absence of cushingoid appearance does not mean that the patient is not at risk of adrenal suppression. However, if a child has cushingoid appearance, he/she should be assumed to have adrenal suppression. The absence of clinical symptoms of adrenal insufficiency does not mean that the patient is not at risk of adrenal suppression. Flow chart summary of management and monitoring of children on long term oral steroid therapy All children commencing long term steroid or treated for > 6 months Steroid card/sick day plan (IM hydrocortisone education ideally) If planning to discontinue long term steroid therapy Wean treatment dose of steroid down to Prednisolone equivalent of 2.5 mg/m2/day over 4-6 Convert to oral hydrocortisone 10 mg/m2/day in three divided doses Need to double dose of oral hydrocortisone (48 hours) during acute illness Inform endocrine team (page 18301) or link endocrine consultant for specialty Synacthen test after at least 8 weeks of oral hydrocortisone - Omit hydrocortisone the night before and morning of synacthen test - Recommence hydrocortisone until results of synacthen test available - Inform endocrine team if peak cortisol to synacthen ≤ 450 nmol/L and review in endocrine clinic Management of children maintained on prolonged (> 6 months) oral steroid (> 2.5 mg/m2/day Prednisolone or > 10 mg/m2/day hydrocortisone equivalent) An investigation of adrenal axis in this group of children whilst they remain on steroid is not necessary as these children have definite secondary adrenal insufficiency. The treatment dose of steroid of is greater than double the physiological dose. However, all children on oral steroid and who are likely to remain on treatment for > 6 months should be: Issued with steroid card/medical bracelet. Counselled not to discontinue steroid abruptly. Provided with sick day plan during intercurrent illnesses, especially when unable to tolerate steroids due to vomiting. Ideally, families should be provided with education to be able to inject IM hydrocortisone in such instances or have immediate access to IM hydrocortisone as per the recommendations of the British Society for Paediatric Endocrinology & Diabetes (BSPED) and the Scottish Paediatric Endocrine Group (SPEG). Provided with IV hydrocortisone cover during acute inpatient admission, surgery, and general anaesthetic. (a) Stress doses of oral steroid (ie double of oral dose of steroid for 2 days) during mild acute illness are not needed for children on ≥ 2.5 mg/m 2 /day Prednisolone or ≥ 10 mg/m 2 /day hydrocortisone equivalent . (b) For children managed with on/off steroid therapy (eg 10 days on/off etc), an oral sick day plan may be needed during the period the child is not on steroid treatment. This could be in the form of 48 hours of usual steroid therapy or in the form of oral hydrocortisone 20 mg/m 2 /day TDS. (c) Stress doses of oral steroid (ie double of oral dose of steroid for 2 days) during mild acute illness are needed for children on ≤ 2.5 mg/m 2 /day Prednisolone or ≤ 10 mg/m 2 /day hydrocortisone equivalent. Dose of Regular Steriod Sick day/stress dose ≥ 5 mg/m 2 /day Prednisolone Or ≥ 10 mg/m 2 /day hydrocortisone equivalent* . No additional increase in dose ≤ 2.5 mg/m 2 /day Prednisolone or ≤ 10 mg/m 2 /day hydrocortisone equivalent*. Double dose of steroids for 48 hours * see equivalent doses here Management of children discontinuing prolonged (> 6 months) oral steroid Normal endogenous cortisol secretion resumes in 6-8 weeks in most cases although normal secretion may not resume for 6-12 months especially in those following prolonged periods of oral steroid treatment (> 12 months) and/or those who have had concurrent treatment with other forms of steroid (eg topical, inhaled or intra-articular etc). 42% of children who discontinued long term oral steroid therapy have an abnormal response to synacthen test despite a weaning regime. No clinical or biochemical factors could predict those with abnormal response ( Wildi-Runge S et al J Pediatr 2013 ). All children should be: Issued with steroid card/medical bracelet. Counselled not to discontinue steroid abruptly. Provided with sick day plan during intercurrent illnesses, especially when unable to tolerate steroids due to vomiting. Ideally, families should be provided with education to be able to inject IM hydrocortisone in such instances or have immediate access to IM hydrocortisone as per the recommendations of the British Society for  Paediatric Endocrinology & Diabetes (BSPED) and the Scottish Paediatric Endocrine Group(SPEG). Provided with IV hydrocortisone cover during acute inpatient admission, surgery, and general anaesthetic. 1. Discontinuing steroid (Duration of treatment > 6 months) These children are at a higher risk of secondary adrenal suppression and therefore a longer recommended period of weaning may be necessary. Wean steroid dose down to a physiological dose  equivalent  (ie 2.5 mg/m 2 /day Prednisolone or equivalent) in the duration that symptoms of the underlying condition permits (or at least 4-6 weeks), then change to hydrocortisone (10 mg/m 2 /day Hydrocortisone) as it has a shorter half-life and aids in the recovery of adrenal function. Inform endocrinology team. Once the child has been on physiological dose of oral hydrocortisone for at least 8 weeks, perform synacthen test. Omit evening and morning dose of hydrocortisone to perform synacthen test. Recommence oral hydrocortisone after synacthen test until results of synacthen test available. Consider discussing weaning plan with endocrinology earlier for children who have been treated with steroid for > 12 months or younger children (< 5 years). 2. Discontinuing steroid (Duration of treatment ≤ 6 months or intermittent treatment eg multiple short courses) Some of these patients may be at risk of adrenal suppression. For safe practice, we recommend the consideration of  synacthen test in the children in this group when off steroids for at least 2 weeks or just before next steroid treatment if there are symptoms of suggestive of adrenal insufficiency or other clinical concerns*. * Symptoms of adrenal insufficiency include: Significantly tired/lethargy Weight gain/weight loss Multiple and increased frequency of intercurrent illnesses (Taking longer to recover) INTERPRETATION OF SYNACTHEN TEST 1. Peak synacthen > 450nmol/L Normal No need for further investigations unless clinical concerns. 2. Peak synacthen 300-450nmol/L Mild to moderate adrenal suppression Inform endocrinology and refer to endocrine clinic. Sick day plan Stress dose oral hydrocortisone (double oral dose for 2 days) for mild acute illness. IM hydrocortisone for vomiting illness. Repeat synacthen test in 6 months if remain off steroids. 3. Peak synacthen < 300 nmol/L Significant adrenal suppression Inform endocrinology and refer to endocrine clinic. Replacement and Sick Day Plan Recommence oral hydrocortisone at physiological dose 10 mg/m2/day. Stress dose oral hydrocortisone (double oral dose for 2 days) for mild acute illness. IM hydrocortisone for vomiting illness. Repeat synacthen test in 6-12 months if remain off steroids. Emergency management of adrenal crisis INTRAMUSCULAR HYDROCORTISONE REGIME FOR VOMITING ILLNESS (FOLLOW SICK DAY PLAN, PARENTS SHOULD BE AWARE) Age IM Hydrocortisone Dose <6months 12.5mg 6 months-5years 25mg 5-10years 50mg >10years 100mg Hospital management of children with secondary adrenal suppression during severe illness Management of children with secondary adrenal suppression due to steroid treatment during acute illness requiring admission is the same as any child with primary adrenal insufficiency. If severely unwell, Check blood sugar and urea & electrolytes including full blood count If capillary glucose <3mmol/l give 2-4 ml/kg of 10% dextrose Fluid bolus may also be required (10-20ml/kg 0.9% saline) if indicated. Give hydrocortisone bolus and start infusion (table below). Give bolus IV hydrocortisone if unwell even if IM hydrocortisone has been given at home. Start IV maintenance fluids + deficit (with dextrose containing fluids) Consider double dose hydrocortisone therapy once able to tolerate oral medications Child may already be on double hydrocortisone therapy and possibly received intramuscular dose of hydrocortisone at home. Beware clinical improvement may be due to IM hydrocortisone. If the child has received a hydrocortisone bolus, either at home or in hospital, we would advise at least overnight admission. Age Hydrocortisone Bolus [if no IM dose given] Hydrocortisone infusion [50mg hydrocortisone in 50mls 0.9%saline] <6months 12.5mg 1ml/hr 6 months-5years 25mg 1ml/hr 5-10years 50mg 2ml/hr >10years 100mg 3ml/hr Management of children with secondary adrenal suppression during surgery For minor surgery/procedure (< 1 hour), bolus IV hydrocortisone should be given at induction (See table above). When the child is able to eat and drink, give usual steroid dose or stress dose oral steroid for the next 24-48 hours (hydrocortisone 20 mg/m 2 /day or equivalent) if usually on hydrocortisone or equivalent of 10 mg/m 2 /day. Beware of children undergoing tonsillectomy, as may not tolerate intake and may need hydrocortisone infusion. For major surgery especially major bowel surgery where the child has to be NBM after surgery, bolus hydrocortisone should be given at induction and a hydrocortisone infusion commenced. When the child is able to eat and drink, give usual steroid dose or stress dose oral steroid for the next 48 hours (hydrocortisone 20 mg/m 2 /day or equivalent). Editorial Information Last reviewed: 25/05/2022 Next review date: 25/05/2023 Author(s): Jarod Wong. Version: 3 Approved By: Paediatric Drugs & Therapeutic Committee Document Id: 511

documents.title: Adrenaline Auto Injector Prescription, Paediatric Allergy Service (142)
documents.content: Adrenaline Auto Injector Prescription, Paediatric Allergy Service (142) ! Warning Objectives The document provides guidance on the prescription of adrenaline auto injectors (AAI) for children. Scope The guidance should be used by healthcare professionals managing children at risk of severe allergic reactions/anaphylaxis. Introduction The prescription of an adrenaline auto injector should be on the basis of a risk assessment which indicates a significant risk of anaphylaxis. This should only be considered; As part of a full allergy assessment including identification of triggers, education on avoidance, assessment of risk and the provision of an allergy management plan or whilst a full assessment is awaited if risk deemed considerable Where adequate training in appropriate usage has been given Where referral or follow-up has been arranged and where rationale for prescription can be reviewed and/or training re-enforced The British Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology has published a detailed guideline for prescribing an AAI and it is available on line for further information ( Adrenaline Auto-Injector - BSACI ). Definitions Mild to moderate allergic reaction is characterized by one or more symptoms or signs of skin and/or gastrointestinal tract involvement without respiratory and/or cardiovascular involvement. Anaphylaxis is a serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death. Severe anaphylaxis is characterized by potentially life-threatening compromise in airway, breathing and/or the circulation, and may occur without typical skin features or circulatory shock being present. Indications for Adrenaline Auto injector Absolute indications for AAI: Previous anaphylaxis* triggered by food, latex or aeroallergen Previous exercise-induced anaphylaxis Previous idiopathic anaphylaxis Co-existing unstable or moderate-to-severe persistent asthma and a food allergy* Hymenoptera venom (bee and wasp stings) allergy in untreated patients (not receiving immunotherapy) with more than cutaneous/mucosal systemic reactions or high risk of re-exposure. * Excluding oral allergy syndrome (OAS or pollen food allergy syndrome) unless patient has previously experienced systemic symptoms . The OAS is generally considered to be a mild form of food allergy; mild irritant symptoms such as itching of the mouth, lips and throat when eating raw fruits and vegetables. Relative indications are (especially if more than one is present): 1) Previous mild-to-moderate allergic reaction to traces of food* 2) Previous mild-to-moderate allergic reaction* to foods known to be associated with anaphylaxis (e.g. peanut and/or tree nut, cow's milk etc.). 3) Teenager or young adult with a food allergy with previous mild-to-moderate reactions* 4) Remote from medical help or prolonged travel abroad in the context of previous mild-to-moderate allergic reactions to a food, hymenoptera venom (bee and wasp stings), latex or aeroallergens * Excluding OAS unless patient has previously experienced systemic symptoms Targeted advice on AAI prescription for allergy specialists; Additional absolute and relative indications Absolute indications During and after venom immunotherapy, in patients with more than cutaneous/mucosal systemic reactions if risk factors for relapse are present. Underlying systemic mastocytosis; children with very severe skin involvement (>50% body surface) and increased basal serum Tryptase levels (>20 ng/ml) and with blistering in the first three years of life. Relative indications Oral immunotherapy for food allergy Hymenoptera venom or drug allergy in patients with more than cutaneous/mucosal systemic reactions and cardiovascular disease Age and Weight based prescription of AAI * Infants at HIGH risk of accidental exposure and who weigh more than 7.5 kg can be issued with a junior AAI (0.15mg). For infants less than 6 months of age, allergen avoidance measures should be effective in most cases. ** Product not available, see BNFc important Safety Information *** if > 60 kg; if small or pre-pubertal offer 0.3 mg Number of AAIs Patients should be given a prescription for 4 devices; two in the emergency bag (giving the option of administering 2 doses) and two for the nursery/school. Editorial Information Last reviewed: 01/11/2022 Next review date: 30/11/2026 Author(s): George Raptis. Approved By: Stakeholders: Specialist Allergy Nurses; Medical Team; Pharmacy; Respiratory Team Document Id: 142 References Emergency treatment of anaphylactic reactions: Guidelines for healthcare providers ; Working Group of Resuscitation Council UK May 2021 EAACI guidelines: Anaphylaxis (2021 update) World Allergy Organisation Anaphylaxis Committee. Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020 Adrenaline Auto-Injector – British Society Allergy Clinical Immunology (2016) BNFc

documents.title: Antibiotic management of suspected or confirmed invasive Group A Streptococcus (iGAS) infection in children
documents.content:
[Page 1] CLINICAL GUIDELINE 
 
 
 
 
 
A guideline is intended to assist healthcare professionals in the choice of disease-specific treatments. 
 
Clinical judgement should be exercised on the applicability of any guideline, influenced by individual patient 
characteristics. Clinicians should be mindful of the potential for harmful polypharmacy and increased 
susceptibility to adverse drug reactions in patients with multiple morbidities or frailty. 
 
If, after discussion with the patient or carer, there are good reasons for not following a guideline, it is good 
practice to record these and communicate them to others involved in the care of the patient. 
 
 
 
 
Version Number: 
1 
Are there changes to the clinical 
content of this version: 
 
Date Approved: 
 
Date of Next Review: 
 
Lead Author: 
Susan Kafka, Advanced Pharmacist Paediatric Antimicrobials 
Approval Group: 
Antimicrobial Utilisation Committee 
 
 
 
 
Important Note: 
 
The Intranet version of this document is the only version that is maintained. 
Any printed copies should therefore be viewed as ‘Uncontrolled’ and as such, may not necessarily contain 
the latest updates and amendments. 
    Antibiotic management of suspected 
or confirmed invasive Group A 
Streptococcus (iGAS) infection in 
children
[Page 2] Greater Glasgow and Clyde Paediatric Antimicrobial Management Team, December 2022. Review 1st March 2023 
 
 
 
Antibiotic management of suspected or confirmed invasive Group A Streptococcus 
(iGAS) infection in children  
 
The purpose of this guidance is to direct the antimicrobial management of suspected or confirmed 
invasive Group A Streptococcus (iGAS) infections in children presenting to the Royal Hospital for 
Children, Glasgow.  Diagnosis and wider clinical management are not within the scope of this 
guidance. 
 
For the management of suspected non-invasive GAS infection please continue to use guidance 
issued by the Scottish Antimicrobial Prescribing Group (SAPG) – accessed via Paediatric Stewardship 
(sapg.scot) 
and that issued by NHS GG&C – accessed via Antibiotic management of Group A Streptococcus 
(GAS, Strep. pyogenes) infection in children (scot.nhs.uk) 
 
The UKHSA and PHS have reported on an unusually high number of children presenting with lower 
respiratory tract GAS infection, including pulmonary empyema.  A large proportion of cases have 
indicated co-infection with respiratory viruses including RSV, influenza, human metapneumovirus 
(hMPV) and enterovirus.  
 
Increased case numbers of GAS and invasive Group A streptococcus infection (iGAS) have placed an 
unprecedented pressure on the medication supply chain.  Alternative antibiotic management 
choices, and practical advice on the use of solid oral dosage forms is included within this guidance. 
 
Isolates of GAS reported within NHS GGC have demonstrated good susceptibility to penicillin and 
macrolide antibiotics.
[Page 3] Greater Glasgow and Clyde Paediatric Antimicrobial Management Team, December 2022. Review 1st March 2023 
 
 
 
Antibiotic management of suspected or confirmed invasive Group A Streptococcus (iGAS) infection in children 
Suspected iGAS sepsis/Toxic Shock Syndrome 
 
1st line: 
IV Ceftriaxone PLUS IV Clindamycin 
Consider IVIG (discuss with ID team) 
Penicillin allergy: 
IV Vancomycin PLUS IV Clindamycin PLUS IV Gentamicin 
 
Review blood cultures at 48hours.  
If GAS confirmed, Ceftriaxone can be switched to Benzylpenicillin.  
Clindamycin can be stopped after 5 days.  
Treatment duration: minimum 2 weeks. Consider IVOST after 7 days if 
improving.  
 
IVOST** (where NO documented penicillin allergy)   
1st line PO Penicillin V 
2nd line PO Amoxicillin 
3rd line PO Co-amoxiclav (only where Penicillin V/Amoxicillin unavailable) 
IVOST in Penicillin allergy: Clarithromycin 
 
If other bacterial sepsis treat as per guidelines or ID/micro advice. If 
culture negative review diagnosis and need for antibiotics. 
Suspected iGAS with severe pneumonia +/- empyema* 
 
1st line: 
IV Cefuroxime PLUS IV Clindamycin 
Penicillin allergy: 
IV Vancomycin PLUS IV Clindamycin PLUS IV Gentamicin 
 
Consider early aggressive source control. 
Review when blood and other cultures available.  
If GAS confirmed: Switch Cefuroxime to IV Benzylpenicillin.  
Continue Clindamycin for a minimum of 5 days in severe 
infection/empyema.  Longer courses can be considered following 
Consultant review.   
 
Treatment duration: 
Pneumonia – complete 7 days antibiotics. Consider IVOST when 
improving.  
 
Empyema – complete 3-4 weeks antibiotics. Consider IVOST after 7 
days if improving. 
 
IVOST** (where NO documented penicillin allergy)   
- 
Pneumonia and confirmed streptococcal empyema: PO 
Amoxicillin  
- 
Empyema unknown cause– PO Co-Amoxiclav 
 
IVOST in Penicillin allergy: Clarithromycin 
 
*NB Severe pneumonia with no features of streptococcal infection 
and no empyema should be treated with IV Cefuroxime +/- 
Gentamicin as per standard guidance 
**For oral antibiotics consider the use of solid oral dosage forms in 
children aged 5 years and older. 
 
Doses as per the BNF-c.  Use highest doses in recommended range. 
 
Dosing regimens for once or twice daily dosing of Penicillin V or 
Amoxicillin are not recommended due to the short half-life of these 
medications in children.
[Page 4] Greater Glasgow and Clyde Paediatric Antimicrobial Management Team, December 2022. Review 1st March 2023 
 
 
**Advice on the use of solid oral dosage forms in children. 
For all children aged 5 year and above, assess for ability to swallow tablets/capsules.  Penicillin tablets are small and easily swallowed using good technique.  
Advice can be found at Healthier Together | Pill Swallowing (Kidzmed) (nenc-healthiertogether.nhs.uk), along with practical information for parents/carers. 
 
 
Where children cannot swallow tablets/capsules an 
alternative treatment option should be chosen. 
 
 
Guidance on the use of solid oral dosage forms can be found 
at: 
https://www.sps.nhs.uk/articles/using-solid-oral-dosage-
form-antibiotics-in-children/ 
 
 
General principles: 
 
 
Ensure the person manipulating the tablet/capsule 
does NOT have a documented penicillin allergy 
 
Use closed systems (eg. barrel of syringe) where 
possible. 
 
Crushed/dispersed oral solid dosage forms can have 
a bitter taste.  This can be masked with a small 
amount of blackcurrant juice (draw up in to the 
syringe), apple sauce or jam. 
 
Administer immediately
[Page 5] Greater Glasgow and Clyde Paediatric Antimicrobial Management Team, December 2022. Review 1st March 2023

documents.title: Antibiotic Therapy in Children: Empirical Recommendations (1288)
documents.content: Antibiotic Therapy in Children: Empirical Recommendations (1288) ! Warning This policy is intended to guide prescribers on appropriate treatment of infections in children at the Royal Hospital for Children, Glasgow. For antibiotic guidance for children in primary care in NHSGGC see Empiric infection management, Primary Care, Paediatric (227) Please also consult local unit guidance, including for patients in the Haematology/Oncology Ward (Schiehallion), the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) and the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). In patients with complex co-morbidities, check for an existing antimicrobial plan. General Principles Starting antibiotics Appropriate specimens for culture (microbiology) should be taken whenever possible before administering antibiotics, however this will depend upon the severity of the illness and the nature of the specimen. In patients who are stable and not septic, and in whom infection is only one of several possibilities, consideration should be given to deferring antibiotics until the results of cultures are known if there is no change in the clinical condition in the interim. If patients are known to be colonised with or have previously cultured MRSA or other multi-drug-resistant organisms, discuss antibiotic management with a Consultant Microbiologist or Consultant in Paediatric Infectious Diseases. Antibiotic dosing Doses of antibiotics are recommended in the BNF for Children (BNFc). Dose according to the clinical indication. Caution should be applied in renal/liver impairment. For dose adjustments see the BNFc or contact a Paediatric Pharmacist for advice. Add a ‘Clinical indication’ when prescribing on electronic/paper drug charts. Add a ‘Stop date’ where possible. In children where isolates are reported as ‘I’ on culture (microbiology) this indicates that a specific dosing schedule is required for the antibiotic to effectively treat the infecting organism. See the Paediatric Isolate guidance for further information. Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with the Infectious Diseases (ID)/Microbiology teams if a prolonged course of IV antibiotics is required. If prescribed empirical cefotaxime, consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when the patient is stable with clinical improvement. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. IV to Oral Switch Therapy (IVOST) The need for antibiotics and their route of administration should be reviewed daily. Some antibiotics have high oral bioavailability and the IV route should only be used if patients are unable to take oral medications. Metronidazole, clindamycin and co-trimoxazole have over 90% oral bioavailability, ciprofloxacin has 70 – 80% oral bioavailability.  Please be aware that oral liquid clindamycin may be difficult to obtain from community pharmacies and may need to be prescribed and dispensed from the hospital. Antibiotics should be rationalised when culture (microbiology) results become available at 48 to 72 hours. When clinically reasonable, consider changing from intravenous (IV) to oral therapy. Refer to the Paediatric IV to oral switch therapy (IVOST) guidance. In patients who are clinically stable, but who can’t be switched to oral antibiotics, consider referral to the Out-patient Parenteral Antibiotic Therapy (OPAT) Service for completion of therapy. Further advice Further advice on antimicrobial prescribing can be obtained from a Consultant Microbiologist, a Consultant in Paediatric Infectious Diseases or the Paediatric Antimicrobial Pharmacist. Infection control advice may be given by a Consultant Microbiologist or the Infection Prevention and Control team. Penicillin allergy Drug allergy refers to immunologically mediated drug hypersensitivity reactions. These may be either immediate (IgE-mediated) or non-immediate (non-IgG mediated) reactions. Most non-IgE mediated are type 4 T-cell mediated reactions. Approach Take a detailed drug allergy history, review the patient’s clinical records, including alerts, and prior prescriptions. Presentation In IgE-mediated reactions symptoms typically develop within 1 hour of drug administration. Reactions can occur days or weeks into a course of treatment. Patients may present with urticaria, angioedema (oedema of the skin or mucous membranes, commonly lips and eyelids), conjunctivitis, rhinitis, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Patients may progress rapidly to anaphylaxis, with cardiorespiratory compromise. Non-IgE-mediated reactions classically present with a symmetrical maculopapular rash sparing the palms and soles. This is often within 6 to 10 days after the first drug exposure, or within 3 days of the second drug exposure, but can occur before these times. Non-IgE mediated reactions can also present as severe reactions with systemic involvement, with mucosal changes (Steven-Johnson's syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and drug-related eosinophilia with systemic symptoms (DRESS)). History not consistent with penicillin allergy Children with the following have no increased risk of an allergic reaction on re-exposure, and the penicillin allergy label can be removed (patient delabelled) A family history but no personal history of penicillin allergy (this is not a risk factor for penicillin allergy). The patient has taken and tolerated (no reaction) the same penicillin after the reported reaction. Symptoms that reflect dose-related reactions rather than antibiotic allergy Minor gastrointestinal symptoms e.g. nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea Oral thrush (Candidiasis) Headache, arthralgia, strange taste in mouth Penicillin allergy If the history is consistent with drug allergy, document this in the clinical records and on the patient prescription. Treat the patient with the penicillin allergy recommendation. Avoid β-lactam antibiotics (including penicillin V/phenoxymethylpenicillin, amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) and first generation cephalosporins (including cephalexin). Second and third generation cephalosporins (including cefuroxime, cefotaxime and ceftriaxone), carbapenems (including meropenem) and monobactams (aztreonam) can be used with caution in an emergency or in patients with severe infections if there is no recommended alternative and no history of an immediate (IgE-mediated) allergy including anaphylaxis, or a severe non-IgE-mediated allergy (including SJS, TEN and DRESS) to penicillin.  If prescribed, the patient should be monitored closely after administration. Examples of antibiotics that are safe in penicillin allergy Tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline), aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin), macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin, azithromycin, erythromycin), quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), glycopeptides (e.g. vancomycin, teicoplanin), trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole, metronidazole, clindamycin and linezolid. This is not an exhaustive list. Drug allergy clinic Discuss referral to the drug allergy clinic with the Paediatric Infectious Diseases, Immunology or Allergy team. If indicated, dictate a referral letter to the drug allergy clinic. Central Nervous System (CNS) Infection Bacterial Meningitis Encephalitis Cerebral Abscess/Subdural Empyema Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis CSF Shunt Infection Bacterial Meningitis Always refer to senior staff to perform an initial assessment to ensure that: Intravenous antibiotics are started as soon as bacterial meningitis is suspected, within 1 hour of arrival in hospital. Unless contraindicated, lumbar puncture is performed before starting antibiotics. Seek ID/microbiology advice about every case of confirmed bacterial meningitis. For suspected meningococcal infection inform the NHS GGC Public Health Protection Team on 64917 Mon-Fri 9-5pm, or via the RHC hospital switchboard and ask for the on-call team out of hours, to discuss contact tracing and antibiotic prophylaxis. Treatment: For suspected bacterial meningitis when the causative organism has not been identified (whilst awaiting test results): Age < 1 month IV Cefotaxime* + IV Gentamicin** + IV Amoxicillin (Use IV Amoxicillin dose in BNFc for Listeria Meningitis, stop if cultures do not grow Listeria spp. after 48 hours). Age 1 month and above IV Cefotaxime* Dexamethasone: For children over 3 months with strongly suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis, give intravenous dexamethasone. For babies between 28 days and 3 months old with strongly suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis, discuss with ID. When the causative organism is found: continue dexamethasone if it is pneumococcus or Haemophilus influenzae type b stop dexamethasone for all other organisms. If no causative organism is found, discuss with ID on whether or not to continue dexamethasone. For children receiving dexamethasone: give the first dose with or before the first dose of antibiotics if possible however, do not delay antibiotics to wait for dexamethasone to be started if dexamethasone is delayed for less than 12 hours after the start of antibiotics, give dexamethasone as soon as possible if dexamethasone is delayed for more than 12 hours after the start of antibiotics, discuss with ID to decide whether dexamethasone is still likely to provide benefit. If true penicillin allergy: Consult ID/Microbiology for advice. Rationalise antibiotic choice according to results of CSF studies (CSF culture, bacterial & viral PCR). If multi-drug-resistant bacteria are identified consult ID/Microbiology. * Consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when stable and clinical improvement. A higher dose of ceftriaxone is indicated for meningitis - see BNFc for dosing. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. ** Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: If bacterial meningitis is suspected but the causative organism is unknown (CSF culture & PCR testing negative), continue IV antibiotics for 10 days.  If under 3 months of age, consider treating with IV antibiotics for 14 days. Discuss with ID/Microbiology if required. When the causative organism is known, minimum duration IV antibiotics as below. If ongoing clinical concerns on completion of treatment course, discuss with ID/Microbiology. Streptococcus pneumoniae : 10 days Haemophilus influenzae type B: 7-10 days Group B streptococcus : 14 days Enterobacterales (coliforms) e.g. E. coli : 21 days Listeria monocytogene s: 21 days. Discuss with ID/Microbiology Neisseria meningitidis : 5 days Treatment Notes Treatment is all with IV antibiotics. PO antibiotic therapy is not appropriate to treat CNS infection. Consider Tuberculosis (TB) meningitis if risk factors for TB infection. Typical CSF findings in TB meningitis include very high protein, low glucose and raised CSF WCC count (predominantly lymphocytes). Any child in whom TB meningitis is considered should be discussed with the ID team immediately. Consider Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) meningoencephalitis in infants < 1 month of age. Common features of HSV disease include presentation with sepsis in the first 2 weeks of life (median age 8 days), encephalopathy, seizures, fever, vesicles (>70% infants with HSV disease have no skin, eye or mouth lesions), raised ALT/AST, coagulopathy. Consider if recent maternal HSV disease but note that around 80% infants with HSV disease are born to women with no history of genital herpes. See the BPSU study. In older children consider HSV disease if focal seizures and encephalopathy. Send EDTA blood and CSF for HSV PCR. See section on Encephalitis . Encephalitis Consider Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) meningoencephalitis in infants < 1 month of age. Common features of HSV disease include presentation with sepsis in the first 2 weeks of life (median age 8 days), encephalopathy, seizures, fever, vesicles (>70% infants with HSV disease have no skin, eye or mouth lesions), raised ALT/AST, coagulopathy. Consider if recent maternal HSV disease but note that around 80% infants with HSV disease are born to women with no history of genital herpes. See the BPSU study. For older children consider HSV disease if focal seizures and encephalopathy. Send EDTA blood and CSF for HSV PCR. If high suspicion of HSV encephalitis and initial CSF HSV PCR is negative, CSF HSV PCR testing should be repeated over 72 hours into illness. Treatment : IV Aciclovir (ensure adequate hydration) Duration: If confirmed HSV in CSF, repeat LP after minimum duration of: 21 days (immunocompromised or age <12 years) 14 days (immunocompetent and age >=12 years) If LP positive, continue aciclovir for a further 7 days then repeat LP. If remains positive after 21 days/28 days, discuss with ID/virology. Following neonatal HSV infection - PO aciclovir prophylaxis for 6 months. Cerebral Abscess/Subdural Empyema Discuss all cases with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: IV Cefotaxime* + IV/PO Metronidazole If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV/PO Ciprofloxacin ** + IV/PO Metronidazole *Consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when stable and clinical improvement. A higher dose of ceftriaxone is indicated for CNS disease - see BNFc dosing recommendation for severe infection/bacterial meningitis. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. **Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: Minimum 6 weeks for aspirated or conservatively treated brain abscess & subdural empyema. Minimum 4 weeks for excised brain abscess. Stop metronidazole after a total of 4 weeks. Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis Refer to Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis guideline for further details on management. Discuss all cases with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: IV Cefotaxime* + IV/PO Metronidazole If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV/PO Ciprofloxacin ** + IV/PO Metronidazole *Consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when stable and clinical improvement. A higher dose of ceftriaxone is indicated for CNS disease - see BNFc dosing recommendation for severe infection/bacterial meningitis. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. **Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics Duration: Minimum 3 weeks for extradural infection & minimum 6 weeks for subdural infection. Stop metronidazole after a total of 4 weeks. CSF Shunt Infection Discuss all cases with ID/Microbiology. Treatment Patient must be fasted and discussed with neurosurgery urgently for consideration of removal of VP shunt. IV Cefotaxime* + IV Vancomycin If true penicillin allergy: IV Meropenem & IV Vancomycin *Consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when stable and clinical improvement. A higher dose of ceftriaxone is indicated for CNS disease - see BNFc dosing recommendation for severe infection/bacterial meningitis. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. Duration: 10 – 14 days if shunt removed. Immunocompromised Patient Immunocompromised plus Sepsis Refer to Management of neutropenia and fever: antibiotic policy if patient is known to the Haematology / Oncology team and discuss with the on-call team. For immunocompromised / immunosuppressed patients known to other hospital specialties see documented individualised plan or discuss with the primary team. For previously unknown patients with febrile neutropenic sepsis: Treatment: IV Piperacillin/Tazobactam + IV Gentamicin* If Staphylococcal infection is suspected (e.g. line-related sepsis or soft tissue infection) ADD IV Vancomycin. If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV Gentamicin* *Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration on advice from ID/Microbiology. Sepsis of Unknown Origin Community-acquired Hospital-acquired Suspected iGAS sepsis/Toxic Shock Syndrome Community-acquired For suspected meningococcal infection Inform the NHS GGC Public Health Protection Team on 64917 Mon-Fri 9-5pm, or via the hospital switchboard and ask for the on-call team out of hours, to discuss contact tracing and antibiotic prophylaxis. Treatment: Age < 1 month IV Cefotaxime* + IV Gentamicin** + IV Amoxicillin (Use IV Amoxicillin dose in BNFc for Listeria Meningitis, stop if cultures do not grow Listeria spp. after 48 hours). Consider Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) in infants < 1 month of age. Common features of HSV disease include presentation with sepsis in the first 2 weeks of life (median age 8 days), encephalopathy, seizures, fever, vesicles (>70% infants with HSV disease have no skin, eye or mouth lesions), raised ALT/AST, coagulopathy. Consider if recent maternal HSV disease but note that around 80% infants with HSV disease are born to women with no history of HSV. See the BPSU study. Send EDTA blood and CSF for HSV PCR. See section on Encephalitis. Start IV aciclovir if any concern of disseminated HSV. If true penicillin allergy: Consult ID/Microbiology for advice. Age 1 month and above IV Cefotaxime* + consider addition of IV Gentamicin** if severe If true penicillin allergy: Consult ID/Microbiology for advice. *Consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when stable and clinical improvement. See BNFc dosing recommendation. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. **Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration (for all ages): When the causative organism is known, minimum duration IV antibiotics as below. If ongoing clinical concerns on completion of treatment course, discuss with ID/Microbiology. If diagnosed with bacteraemia and meningitis use duration recommended for meningitis. If no CSF result but clinical concern about meningitis at presentation, use duration recommended for meningitis. Staphylococcus aureus MSSA: 14 days Staphylococcus aureus MRSA: 14 days Streptococcus pneumoniae : 7-10 days (Meningitis 10 days) Group A Streptococcus: 7-10 days Group B streptococcus : 7 days (Meningitis 14 days) Haemophilus influenzae type B : 7-10 days (Meningitis 7-10 days) Enterobacterales (coliforms) e.g. E. coli : 7 - 10 days (Meningitis 21 days) Neisseria meningitidis : 5 days (Meningitis 5 days) If multi-drug-resistant bacteria cultured discuss with ID/Microbiology. If concern about clinical response to treatment discuss with ID. IVOST to complete the total antibiotic course may be considered in bacteraemia associated with bone and joint infection, urinary tract infection, and lower respiratory tract infection. This should be discussed with ID/Microbiology. Hospital-acquired If central venous access device (CVAD) check for an individualised plan for suspected CVAD line sepsis. Please review all relevant prior culture results, discuss with ID/Microbiology if multi-drug-resistant organisms cultured. Treatment: Age < 1 month Discuss with ID/Microbiology Age 1 month and above IV Piperacillin/Tazobactam + IV Gentamicin* If true penicillin allergy: Consult ID/Microbiology for advice. If suspected CVAD infection add teicoplanin or vancomycin whilst awaiting blood culture results. If confirmed central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) please refer to the GGC Paediatric Line-Related Sepsis (905) guideline. *Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration on advice from ID/Microbiology. Suspected iGAS sepsis/Toxic Shock Syndrome Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + PO/IV Clindamycin If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV Clindamycin + IV Gentamicin* If suspected toxic shock syndrome or toxin-mediated disease requiring PICU-level care, consider addition of IVIG . Discuss with ID. If suspected Staphylococcus aureus Toxic Shock Syndrome, discuss antibiotics with ID/Microbiology. Review blood cultures at 48hrs. If Group A Streptococcus is confirmed, Cefotaxime can be switched to Benzylpenicillin. *Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: 7 - 10 days Consider stopping Clindamycin after a minimum of 5 days. Lower Respiratory Tract Infection Community-acquired pneumonia – not requiring hospital admission Community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission Aspiration pneumonia Pneumonia complicating influenza (non-severe & severe) Empyema Community-acquired pneumonia 1. Community-acquired pneumonia – not requiring hospital admission If requiring hospital admission, please send a throat swab for an extended respiratory viral PCR test (includes Mycoplasma pneumoniae PCR). If productive cough, please send sputum for bacterial culture. Treatment: PO Amoxicillin If true penicillin allergy: PO Azithromycin* If Mycoplasma pneumoniae likely pathogen (consider if high community prevalence, failure of treatment with amoxicillin after 3 days, children > 5 years, mucocutaneous manifestations): PO Azithromycin* If no clinical improvement after 48 hours antibiotics or pointers to infection with Haemophilus influenza (such as prior culture) discuss antibiotic with ID/microbiology. *Azithromycin has numerous serious drug interactions, see BNFc or contact pharmacy for details. Duration: 5 days (PO Amoxicillin) 3 days (PO Azithromycin) 2. Community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission If multi-drug-resistant or toxin-producing bacteria cultured e.g. PVL- Staphylococcus aureus , discuss with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: PO Co-amoxiclav (IV only if not tolerating oral, or complicated pneumonia e.g. pleural effusion, lung abscess, necrosis). If true penicillin allergy: PO Clarithromycin . If severe disease IV Vancomycin and IV Ciprofloxacin* *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. For lower respiratory tract infection in children with known conditions associated with recurrent infection (e.g. cystic Fibrosis, bronchiectasis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, primary immunodeficiencies, neurodisability) treatment should be guided by the underlying condition and previous microbiology results. Treatment should be discussed with the relevant primary team (e.g. Respiratory, Infectious Diseases/Immunology teams). Duration: 5-7 days Aspiration pneumonia If co-morbidity (e.g. neurodisability) treatment should be guided by the underlying condition and previous microbiology results. Treatment should be discussed with the relevant primary team (e.g. Respiratory, Infectious Diseases/Immunology teams). If no previous resistant organisms cultured, treat as for community-acquired pneumonia. Pneumonia complicating influenza (non-severe & severe) Secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza is often due to Staphylococcus aureus . If not severely unwell, treat as for community-acquired pneumonia. If unwell or signs of sepsis/toxin-mediated disease, discuss with ID/Microbiology. Empyema Discuss source control procedure with the Paediatric General Surgical team. If multi-drug-resistant or toxin-producing bacteria cultured e.g. PVL- Staphylococcus aureus , discuss with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: IV Co-amoxiclav (+ PO/IV Clindamycin if concern about toxin-mediated disease) If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV Ciprofloxacin* (+ PO/IV Clindamycin if concern about toxin-mediated disease). If suspected toxic shock syndrome or toxin-mediated disease requiring PICU-level care, consider IV Cefotaxime + PO/IV Clindamycin , with addition of IVIG . Discuss with ID. IVOST antibiotic choice should be guided by microbiology results. If Group A Streptococcus is cultured, Cefotaxime can be switched to Benzylpenicillin. *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: Total antibiotic duration 2 weeks. If needing longer due to slow response to treatment, discuss with ID. If added Clindamycin to cover for toxin-mediated disease, stop Clindamycin after 5 days. Upper Respiratory Tract Infection Tonsillitis (if antibiotic required) Pertussis Otitis Media Acute Sinusitis Acute Mastoiditis Bacterial tracheitis Epiglottitis Lymphadenitis Deep neck space infection Lemierre’s Syndrome Tonsillitis (if antibiotic required) Refer to Acute sore throat, Paediatric guideline for further information including investigations and clinical decision-making tools to support prescribing decisions and management. If the child has stridor, respiratory distress, drooling or is systemically very unwell, consider urgent review by the ENT and PICU teams and consider diagnoses; severe croup, bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis (see relevant section on guidance) Treatment of tonsillitis: PO Penicillin V (IV Benzylpenicillin if unable to tolerate oral medication) If true penicillin allergy: PO Clarithromycin* (IV if unable to tolerate oral medication) *Clarithromycin has numerous serious drug interactions, see BNFc for details. Duration: 5 days unless symptoms remain at 5 days of treatment, then a further 5 days is indicated. 10 days if relapse/recurrence of tonsilitis within 2 weeks or where there are signs/symptoms of scarlet fever. Pertussis Pertussis remains a notifiable disease in the UK. Suspected and confirmed cases must be notified.  Inform the NHS GGC Public Health Protection Team on 64917 Mon-Fri 9-5pm, or via the hospital switchboard and ask for the on-call team out of hours, to discuss contact tracing and antibiotic prophylaxis (prophylaxis not required for index case). Treatment: PO Clarithromycin * *Clarithromycin has numerous serious drug interactions, see BNFc for details. Duration: 7 days Otitis Media Children with acute otitis media should not be routinely prescribed antibiotics as most cases are viral in aetiology. Immediate antibiotics should only be given if systemically unwell or high risk of complications, or if there is no resolution or deterioration in symptoms over 3 days. Consider antibiotics (immediate or a back-up antibiotic prescription) if perforated ear drum or under 2 years of age with bilateral otitis media, in line with the NICE guideline. Treatment: PO Amoxicillin If worsening symptoms on Amoxicillin taken for at least 2-3 days, recommend clinical review, and consider switching to PO Co-amoxiclav. If true Penicillin allergy: PO Clarithromycin* If no clinical improvement after 48 hours antibiotics or pointers to infection with Haemophilus influenza (such as prior culture) discuss antibiotic with ID/microbiology. *Clarithromycin has numerous serious drug interactions, see BNFc for details. Duration: 5-7 days (PO Amoxicillin) 5-7 days (PO Clarithromycin) Acute Sinusitis Children with acute sinusitis should not be routinely prescribed antibiotics as most cases are viral in aetiology. Immediate antibiotics should only be given if systemically unwell or high risk of complications. If symptoms for 10 days or more consider antibiotic treatment. If complicated by intracranial infection, refer to CNS section (cerebral abscess/subdural effusion or venous sinus thrombosis) & discuss with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: PO Clarithromycin * If severe: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Metronidazole : IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav. If severe and true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin and IV Ciprofloxacin** IVOST antibiotic choice should be guided by microbiology results (including intra-operative sample cultures). *Clarithromycin has numerous serious drug interactions, see BNFc for details. **Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: Minimum 5 days Acute Mastoiditis If complicated by intracranial infection, refer to CNS section (cerebral abscess/subdural effusion or venous sinus thrombosis) & discuss with the ID/Microbiology. Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Metronidazole: IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin and IV Ciprofloxacin* IVOST antibiotic choice should be guided by microbiology results (including intra-operative sample cultures). *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: 14 days total Bacterial tracheitis Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Clindamycin: IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: IV/PO Clindamycin and IV Ciprofloxacin* Discuss IVOST antibiotic choice with ID/Microbiology *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: Minimum 5 days and review. Epiglottitis Treatment: IV Cefotaxime: IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: IV/PO Clindamycin and IV Ciprofloxacin* Discuss IVOST antibiotic choice with ID/Microbiology *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: Minimum 5 days and review. Lymphadenitis Treatment: PO Co-amoxiclav. If severe disease IV Co-amoxiclav. If true penicillin allergy: PO Clindamycin. If severe disease discuss with ID/Microbiology. Consider addition of IV Gentamicin* *Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: 7 days Deep neck space infection Treatment: Consider drainage to attain source control. IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Metronidazole: IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav . If true penicillin allergy: IV/PO Clindamycin + IV Gentamicin *:  IVOST > PO Clindamycin . * Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: 10-14 days Lemierre’s Syndrome If suspected discuss with the ID team. Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Metronidazole: IVOST> PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: IV/PO Clindamycin + IV Gentamicin*: IVOST> PO Clindamycin * Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: Minimum 3 weeks, total duration dependent on clinical response, discuss with ID. Orbital Infections Pre-septal Cellulitis Orbital Cellulitis Pre-septal Cellulitis For further information refer to Preseptal cellulitis in children (1075) Treatment: PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: PO Clindamycin Duration: 7 days Orbital Cellulitis For further information on assessment and management refer to Orbital and periorbital cellulitis in children (225). If complicated by intracranial infection, refer to CNS section (cerebral abscess/subdural effusion or venous sinus thrombosis) & discuss with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV / PO Clindamycin: IVOST > Co-amoxiclav . If true penicillin allergy: IV/PO Clindamycin and IV Ciprofloxacin* If no improvement after 48 hours, add IV/PO Metronidazole whilst awaiting the results of intra-cranial imaging. Discuss IVOST antibiotic choice with ID/Microbiology *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: 10-14 days Gastro-Intestinal Infections Gastroenteritis Appendicitis Intra-abdominal infection Intra-abdominal abscess Cholangitis Helicobacter pylori Infection Clostridium Difficile Infection Gastroenteritis No antibiotics usually required. Appendicitis Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Metronidazole (PO when tolerating oral medications) If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV Ciprofloxacin* + IV/PO Metronidazole ( PO Ciprofloxacin + PO Metronidazole when tolerating oral medications). If concerns about sepsis add IV Gentamicin** IVOST antibiotic choice should be guided by microbiology results (including intra-operative sample cultures). *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. **Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: Simple: 24 hours Complex (perforation, necrosis): 5 days total Intra-abdominal infection Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Metronidazole (PO when tolerating oral medications) If true penicillin allergy: IV Vancomycin + IV Ciprofloxacin* + IV Metronidazole ( PO Ciprofloxacin + PO M etronidazole when tolerating oral medications). If concerns about sepsis add IV Gentamicin** IVOST antibiotic choice should be guided by microbiology results (e.g. intra-operative, ascitic fluid cultures). *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. **Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: Minimum total 5 – 7 days Intra-abdominal abscess Source control most effective. If source control not possible, then discuss with ID/Microbiology. Cholangitis Refer to Cholangitis pathway for further information. Helicobacter pylori Infection Refer to Helicobacter pylori infection guidelines for further information. Clostridium Difficile Infection Refer to CDI guidelines for further information. Urinary Tract See Urinary Tract Infection, Acute Management in Children guideline for definitions of urinary tract infection (UTI), including symptoms suggestive of upper and lower UTI. If a child is known to the renal service or has had previous UTIs then please check previous urine culture results as this may influence empiric antibiotic prescribing decisions. Upper Tract Infection/Pyelonephritis Lower Tract Infection Upper Tract Infection/Pyelonephritis If suspected sepsis, unable to tolerate oral antibiotics or patient below 3 months of age: Treatment: IV Cefotaxime* (consider one-off dose of Gentamicin if suspected sepsis or unwell neonate) If true penicillin allergy: Use Gentamicin** initially and discuss with ID/Microbiology. *Consider switching IV cefotaxime to IV ceftriaxone when stable and clinical improvement. See BNFc dosing recommendation. See cautions/contraindications for ceftriaxone in neonates in the BNFc. **Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: 7-10 days (min 48 hours IV then review for IVOST) If no suspected sepsis, able to tolerate PO antibiotics, in patients 3 months of age and above: Treatment: PO Cefalexin If true penicillin allergy: PO Ciprofloxacin* *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics Duration: 7 days Lower Tract Infection Treatment: PO Cefalexin If true penicillin allergy and over 3 months of age: PO Nitrofurantoin If true penicillin allergy and under 3 months of age: Discuss with ID/Microbiology Duration: 3 days Bone/Joint Infection Septic arthritis / Osteomyelitis If infection is associated with metalwork, please discuss antibiotic choice and duration of treatment with ID/Microbiology. Treatment 1. Age 3 months and below: IV Cefotaxime : IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: Discuss with ID/Microbiology 2. Age 3 months to up to 5 years IV Cefuroxime : IVOST > Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: IV Clindamycin : IVOST> PO Clindamycin . If suspected K. kingae infection *, consider Co-trimoxazole **. Discuss with ID/Microbiology. 3. Age 5 years and above IV Flucloxacillin : IVOST > PO Flucloxacillin or Co-amoxiclav liquid if Flucloxacillin not tolerated If true penicillin allergy: IV Clindamycin : IVOST > PO Clindamycin . 4. If Sickle Cell Disease or no Haemophilus Influenza B vaccine IV Cefotaxime : IVOST > PO Co-amoxiclav If true penicillin allergy: IV Clindamycin and IV Ciprofloxacin*** : IVOST > PO Clindamycin and Ciprofloxacin*** Modify treatment according to culture results & clinical response. Discuss with ID/microbiology. * Consider K. Kingae infection < 5yrs, CRP < 40mg/L, involvement knee or shoulder joint. **Co-trimoxazole is not licenced for use in children <6 weeks of age. Co-trimoxazole can cause blood disorders and electrolyte disturbance. See BNFc for cautions and contraindications for use. Measure baseline bloods (UE, FBC).  If blood test results are abnormal, discuss treatment recommendations and monitoring with ID/Microbiology. If blood tests are normal and treatment duration of oral co-trimoxazole extends beyond 1 week, patients should have repeat blood test monitoring (UE, FBC) at 1 and 2 weeks and then monthly . This can be at a follow-up orthopaedic out-patient appointment or arranged on ward 1C. If unsure, please discuss monitoring requirements and results with ID/Microbiology. Counsel patients and parents/carers about the risk of drug allergy, i.e. that if patients develop a rash whilst taking co-trimoxazole they should stop taking it immediately and seek medical advice. ***Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Duration: 2-3 weeks in septic arthritis, 3-4 weeks in osteomyelitis. For complex disease* or infants under 3 months of age: 6 weeks total (2 weeks IV then PO) or longer if not resolved. *Complex disease: Multifocal, significant bone loss, unusual or resistant pathogen, immunosuppressed patient, sepsis or shocked, infection associated with metalwork. Review all IV antibiotics at 48hrs. IVOST should be considered for osteomyelitis/septic arthritis: when patient is afebrile, pain free for >24 hours and when CRP is <20mg/l or has reduced by 2/3 of its highest value. Ensure no signs of complications (e.g. metastatic foci inc. endocarditis, pneumonia or DVT), no growth of virulent pathogens (e.g. PVL- Staphylococcus aureus) , and negative blood cultures before IVOST. Skin/Soft Tissue Abscess Cellulitis Necrotising Fasciitis Infected Human/Animal bite Abscess Refer to the General Surgical Team – may need incision and drainage. Cellulitis If severe sepsis refer to the section on Sepsis and discuss with ID/Microbiology. If severe cellulitis or pain out of proportion with clinical findings, consider necrotising fasciitis. See the section on Necrotising Fasciitis . In patients with previous culture of MRSA on skin/soft tissue samples please be guided by previous microbiology antibiotic sensitivity results. Isolates may be sensitive to clindamycin or co-trimoxazole. If no available oral antibiotic options discuss antibiotic management with ID/Microbiology. Treatment: IV Flucloxacillin: IVOST > PO Flucloxacillin If true penicillin allergy: IV Clarithromycin * or IV Clindamycin : IVOST > PO Clarithromycin or PO Clindamycin Modify therapy according to culture results and the clinical response. *Clarithromycin has numerous serious drug interactions, see BNFc for more details. Duration: 5-7 days Necrotising Fasciitis Discuss the patient immediately with the paediatric surgical and plastic surgery teams; necrotising fasciitis requires rapid debridement of all infected tissues in combination with empirical antibiotic therapy. A multidisciplinary approach (General Surgery, Plastic Surgery, ID/Microbiology, and PICU) is required. Whilst the patient is waiting for surgery, monitor them for signs of sepsis or toxin-mediated disease, as well as local signs and symptoms of extension of the area of necrotising fasciitis. Treatment: IV Cefotaxime + IV/PO Clindamycin + IV/PO Metronidazole + IV Gentamicin* If true penicillin allergy or if MRSA suspected REPLACE Cefotaxime with Vancomycin In perineal infection consider Piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) in place of cefotaxime if no penicillin allergy, especially if gentamicin is contra-indicated. Discuss with ID/Microbiology if penicillin allergy. If known colonisation with multi-drug-resistant organisms discuss with ID/Microbiology. Rationalise antibiotics in line with culture results and clinical progress. *Gentamicin should not continue beyond 3 doses, discuss with ID/Microbiology if a prolonged course of intravenous antibiotics is required. Duration: 10-14 days total. Consider IVOST when clinical improvement, no spreading infection, afebrile for over 24hrs. Infected Human/Animal bite See NICE guidance for risk stratification and treatment recommendations for bites. Seek specialist advice from ID for bites from a wild or exotic animal or farm animals (including birds and non-traditional pets). Refer to Management of possible rabies exposure in children and young people (1192) in patients who have been bitten by an animal outside of the UK, or by a bat within the UK. Assess the risk of tetanus, rabies or a bloodborne viral infection and take appropriate action. For antibiotic prophylaxis for uninfected bites refer to the NICE guidance . The following recommendations are for infected bites: If there is discharge from the wound, take a swab for microbiological testing to guide treatment. Review antibiotic choice based on swab results. Manage the wound with irrigation and debridement as necessary. Treatment of an infected bite Age below 1 month: Seek advice from ID/Microbiology. Age 1 month and over: PO Co-amoxiclav. If patient is unable to take oral antibiotics or if severely unwell IV Co-amoxiclav may be given. If true penicillin allergy: Age 6 weeks to 11 years: PO Co-trimoxazole. If patient is below 6 weeks of age, seek advice from an ID/Microbiology, as Co-trimoxazole is not licenced for this age group. Age 12 to 17 years: PO Doxycycline + PO Metronidazole . Treatment of deep bites/severe infection/unable to tolerate oral antibiotics Discuss all patients with suspected sepsis with ID/Microbiology IV Co-amoxiclav Penicillin Allergy (low risk; no anaphylaxis after penicillin): IV Cefuroxime + IV/PO Metronidazole (Replace IV Cefuroxim e with IV Cefotaxime if suspected sepsis) Penicillin Allergy (High risk; anaphylaxis or severe systemic reaction after penicillin): IV Vancomycin + IV/PO Ciprofloxacin* + IV/PO Metronidazole *Please see MHRA alert on fluoroquinolone antibiotics Duration: A 5-day course is appropriate for treating most human or animal bites, but course length can be increased to 7 days (with review) based on clinical assessment of the wound, for example, if there is significant tissue destruction or it has penetrated bone, joint, tendon or vascular structures. If the wound is infected — review at 24 and 48 hours to ensure the infection is responding to treatment. If patient is discharged, advice to attend urgently for review if the infection worsens or if they feel increasingly unwell. Editorial Information Last reviewed: 29/07/2026 Next review date: 31/07/2029 Author(s): Shahad Abbas, Paediatric Antimicrobial Pharmacist, Katherine Longbottom, Consultant in Paediatric Infectious Disease, Louisa Pollock, Consultant in Paediatric Infectious Disease.
